input:
It is recommended that a three-month pilot should be carried out before any decision is taken regarding full installation. The pilot is owned by the reliability engineering group, which will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation will be held until such time as the pilot results have been reported.

The plant operates a total of 180 pumps. An analysis of the maintenance records covering a period of 12 months has revealed a total of 1338 h of unplanned downtime, of which bearing failures account for 44% of the downtime hours, equivalent to 589 h. These records constitute the evidence base on which the recommendation rests: the downtime is concentrated within a single failure class, and it is that class which the sensors are designed to address.

In a trial that was conducted by the vendor on a comparable unit, the sensors were found to cut downtime by 24%. It should be noted, however, that this figure is a vendor figure which has not been measured at this plant, and the pilot is intended to replace it with a measurement obtained under plant conditions. Spare-part lead times are not changed by the sensors, so no part of the case is based on any assumption of faster repair.

The pilot will cover 18 pumps and will cost $40k over the three months, whilst full installation has been quoted at $411k installed, plus a further $68k per year. The trade-off can therefore be expressed as the pilot cost set against the quoted full cost: a small and bounded expenditure purchases the measurement on which the larger commitment would rest, and the March review will receive the pilot result before it is asked to approve the installation money.

Recommendation: run the three-month pilot before any decision on full installation. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

The plant runs 180 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1338 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 44% of the downtime hours (589 h). The records are the evidence base for the recommendation: the downtime is concentrated in one failure class, and that class is the one the sensors address.

In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 24%. The figure is a vendor figure; it was not measured at this plant, and the pilot exists to replace it with a plant measurement. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so no part of the case rests on faster repair.

The pilot covers 18 pumps and costs $40k over the three months; full installation is quoted at $411k installed, plus $68k per year. The trade-off is the pilot cost against the quoted full cost: a small, bounded spend buys the measurement on which the larger commitment would rest, and the March review receives the pilot result before it is asked for the installation money.

The pilot report is specified now, so that the review can judge the full installation on plant data. The report carries the downtime hours on the pilot pumps against the same period of the maintenance record, the split of those hours by failure class, and the availability of the sensors over the trial. A pilot that reported only a percentage would repeat the weakness of the vendor figure it replaces.
